title: Sounds, letters and the alphabet
objectives: I can explain why Portuguese spelling is regular, and name the few things that spelling cannot tell me.
I can say the name of every letter and spell my own name aloud.
I can say the seven oral vowels, tell open from closed e and o when an accent mark shows it, and explain how unstressed final vowels change.
I can recognize nasal vowels and diphthongs from the tilde, from m and n, and from the endings ão, ães and ões.
I can apply the spelling rules for c, ç, qu, g, gu, j, s, z, x, r, h, ch, lh, nh, final l and t and d before i, and use them to read a word I have never seen.

vocabulary.note: Acute accent on e. Rule: the accent marks a stressed, open vowel, é [ɛ], like the e in English 'bed'. Say it short and steady, with no glide.
Circumflex on e. Rule: the circumflex marks a stressed, closed vowel, ê [e], like the 'ay' of English 'say' but stopped before the glide. The stress is on the last syllable: be-BÊ [beˈbe].
Acute accent on o. Rule: an accented ó is stressed and open [ɔ], like the 'aw' of English 'law': a-VÓ [aˈvɔ]. It differs from avô, the grandfather, only in this vowel.
Circumflex on o. Rule: an accented ô is stressed and closed [o], like the 'o' of English 'go' without the final 'oo' glide: a-VÔ [aˈvo]. Compare avó.

No accent, yet the stressed o is open [ɔ]: BAW-luh [ˈbɔlɐ]. Rule: spelling cannot tell you whether an unmarked e or o is open or closed (compare bolo, the cake, with a closed o). Final unstressed a is a weak 'uh' [ɐ].
Rule: u is [u], like the 'oo' of English 'moon', with rounded lips and no glide. Final unstressed a is a weak 'uh': OO-vuh [ˈuvɐ].
Tilde on a. Rule: the tilde marks a nasal vowel, and the ending ão is the nasal diphthong [ɐ̃w̃], like 'ow' in 'now' said through the nose: PÃO [pɐ̃w̃]. The plural is pães.
Two rules. Ç (c with a cedilla) is always [s], here before o: li-ÇÃO [liˈsɐ̃w̃]. The ão ending is nasal and the last syllable is stressed. The plural is lições.
Three rules. C before a is [k]; a single s between two vowels is [z], like the 'z' of 'zoo'; final unstressed a is 'uh': KAH-zuh [ˈkazɐ].
Rule: ss between vowels is always [s], a hiss. This is how Portuguese writes [s] where a single s would buzz: MAH-suh [ˈmasɐ]. The word also means dough or batter.
Rule: c before e or i is [s]: see-NAY-muh [siˈnemɐ]. The closed e is slightly nasal because the m that follows starts the next syllable.
Three rules. Qu before e is [k] and the u is silent; the diphthong ei is [ej] like 'ay' in 'day'; j is [ʒ], like the 's' of 'measure'; final o is 'oo': KEI-zhoo [ˈkejʒu].
Three rules. Gu before i is [g] and the u is silent; the i is a plain [i]; rr is the strong guttural sound [h], like a hard English 'h' in 'hat': gee-TAH-huh [giˈtahɐ].
Rule: g before e or i is [ʒ], like the 's' of English 'measure': ZHAY-loo [ˈʒelu]. Final o is 'oo'. Compare gato, where g before a is the hard [g].
Rule: ch is always [ʃ], like English 'sh' in 'shoe', never like the 'ch' of 'church'. Final unstressed e is said like 'ee': SHAH-vee [ˈʃavi].
Rule: lh is one sound [ʎ], like the 'lli' in English 'million': FEE-lyoo [ˈfiʎu]. Do not say an l followed by an h. The plural os filhos can also mean 'the children'.
Rule: nh is one sound [ɲ], like the 'ny' in English 'canyon'. The a before it is lightly nasal: BAH-nyoo [ˈbɐ̃ɲu].
Rule: x at the start of a word is [ʃ], 'sh'. The acute accent marks the stressed syllable: XÍ-ca-ra [ˈʃikaɾɐ]. C before a is [k]; the single r between vowels is a quick tap [ɾ].
Rule: ex followed by a vowel is [ez], so the x is [z], like the 'z' of 'zoo': eh-ZAH-mee [eˈzɐ̃mi]. The a is lightly nasal because the m that follows starts the next syllable. Final e is said 'ee'.
Rule: x between vowels is sometimes [ks], as here: TAH-ksee [ˈtaksi]. Nothing in the spelling tells you this, so learn each such word. The acute accent marks the stressed syllable.
Three rules. Single r after b is a quick tap [ɾ]; s between vowels is [z]; l at the end of a syllable is [w], like the 'w' of 'now': bra-ZIW [bɾaˈziw].
Rule: r at the start of a word is the strong guttural [h], like a strong English 'h' in 'hat': HOO-uh [ˈhuɐ]. Do not use the English r.
Rule: rr between vowels is the same strong guttural [h] as r at the start of a word: KAH-hoo [ˈkahu]. Compare the single r of cara [ˈkaɾɐ], which is a tap.
Rule: h is always silent. The o is open [ɔ] and the single r between vowels is a tap [ɾ]: AW-ruh [ˈɔɾɐ]. The plural as horas is used to tell the time.
Rule: in most of Brazil, d before the sound [i] is said like the 'j' of English 'jeans': JEE-a [ˈdʒiɐ].
Rule: in most of Brazil, t before the sound [i] is said like the 'ch' of English 'cheese': CHEE-a [ˈtʃiɐ].

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why Portuguese can be read aloud from the page
grammar.explanation:
Spelling is a code for sounds. A code works well when each symbol stands for one sound, and English works badly: the letters ough are said in six different ways in though, through, tough, cough, bough and thought, so an English reader memorizes each word separately. Portuguese spelling was arranged to record pronunciation closely. Each letter, or each pair of letters, stands for one sound or a small set of sounds, and when there is a choice, something you can see in the word decides it: the letter that comes next, the position of the letter in the word, or an accent mark. That is the principle behind this whole lesson. Learn the rules once and you can read aloud almost any word you have never met. Every rule has a reason, and the rest of the course relies on them.

Some terms used from here on. A vowel is a sound made with the air flowing freely through the mouth, such as the sound in 'see' or 'go'. A consonant is a sound made by closing or narrowing the mouth somewhere, such as 'p', 's' or 'm'. The letters a, e, i, o, u are the vowel letters; all the others are consonant letters. A syllable is one beat of a word, built around one vowel sound: ca-sa has two syllables and u-ni-ver-si-da-de has six. The stressed syllable is the one said louder, longer and clearer than the others, like 'nan' in English 'banana'. A diacritic is a small mark added to a letter (the tilde ~, the acute accent ´, the circumflex ^, the cedilla ¸), and each one changes a sound or shows stress in a fixed way. Finally, square brackets such as [ʒ] hold symbols of the International Phonetic Alphabet, a system in which each symbol stands for exactly one sound. They are given so you can be exact; every sound is also compared with English, so you can ignore the symbols until they become useful.

Three kinds of letters appear in Portuguese. Some have one steady sound wherever they occur (b, f, p, v and others). Some have a small set of sounds, and the neighbouring letters or the position choose among them (c, g, s, x, r and others); the next notes give the rules. And the diacritics work like letters too: each has a fixed job. Silent letters are rare. Only h is always silent, and u is silent in que, qui, gue and gui. There is nothing like the silent letters of 'knife', 'island' or 'through'. Note also that reading from spelling is more reliable than writing from sound: the sound [s] is written s, ss, c, ç, sc or x in different words, so hearing a word does not always tell you how it is spelled, but seeing a word almost always tells you how to say it.

Spelling cannot tell you a few things, and it is honest to list them now. First, which syllable is stressed. In many words the spelling gives you the answer through a default rule, and in the others an accent mark is written to override the rule; this is the subject of the next lesson. Second, whether a written e or o with no accent mark is open or closed: ela 'she' has an open e [ɛ], ele 'he' has a closed e [e], and bola 'ball' and bolo 'cake' differ in the same way with o. The accent marks solve this when they appear, and the next lesson explains why they appear where they do; without a mark you learn the vowel with the word. Third, the letter x between two vowels: táxi has the sound [ks] and lixo has [ʃ], and the pattern in note 5 only covers some cases. These three gaps are small compared with English, and everything else can be worked out from the rules.

rows: Does the same spelling give the same sound?
Yes, unless a rule you can see picks another sound
Rarely: h, and u in que, qui, gue, gui

Yes, with the rules of this lesson

grammar.title: The alphabet and the names of the letters
grammar.explanation:
The Portuguese alphabet has 26 letters, the same shapes in the same order as the English alphabet. Twenty-three are traditional, and k, w and y are loan letters, meaning letters that come from other languages and are used mostly in foreign words and names (karaokê, watt, Wagner, Yasmin). They became official members of the alphabet through the Orthographic Agreement, which took effect in Brazil in 2009, and Brazilian names that use them are common. A letter is a written symbol. Its name is a word used to say the letter aloud, and the name is different from the sound the letter makes inside words, just as the English name 'double-u' is not the sound of w in 'water'. You need the names whenever you spell something aloud: your name, an email address, a street.

The table gives each name and what it sounds like to an English speaker. Four things are worth noticing. First, the names of a, e and o are said á, é and ó. Alphabet lists print them as a, e, o, but this course writes them á, é, ó whenever they are meant to be spoken, because a bare a, e or o in a sentence is read as one of the short words a 'the', e 'and' or o 'the', which are said with weak vowels (note 3). Second, most consonant names follow one of two patterns: the consonant followed by ê (bê, cê, dê, gê, pê, quê, tê, vê, zê), or é followed by the consonant and a weak final e (efe, ele, eme, ene, erre, esse). A final e is said like 'ee', so efe sounds like EH-fee. Third, the accent marks inside the names (á, ê, é, ó) show which vowel sound is used and that the syllable is stressed; notes 3 and 4 and the next lesson explain the marks. Fourth, the unusual names are agá (h), jota (j), cá (k), dáblio (w), xis (x) and ípsilon (y). In Brazil y is also called i grego, literally 'Greek i', and w is also called vê dobrado, literally 'doubled v'. The letter h is agá, but inside a word h is silent (note 5).

To spell a name aloud, say the letter names in order with a short pause between them. For a repeated letter say both names, or say dois before the plural name: dois erres, literally 'two r's', for rr. Say a mark after the letter it belongs to: á com til for ã, literally 'a with tilde', and cê cedilha for ç. Brazilians often add the word com 'with' or sem 'without' to settle doubtful letters, as in Helena com agá, 'Helena with h'. The examples below spell Ana, Paulo, Bia, Joana, Carlos and the three loan letters.

grammar.title: The vowels: five letters, seven oral sounds, and weak unstressed vowels
grammar.explanation:
A vowel letter is not the same thing as a vowel sound. Portuguese has five vowel letters, a, e, i, o, u, but seven oral vowel sounds. Oral means that the air leaves through the mouth only; nasal vowels, which also use the nose, are in the next note. The count is seven because e and o each spell two sounds, one open and one closed. Open and closed describe the jaw and tongue: for an open vowel the mouth is more open and the jaw lower, and for a closed vowel the jaw rises a little. Say é and then ê in front of a mirror and watch your jaw lift. The difference changes meaning: avó [aˈvɔ] is a grandmother and avô [aˈvo] is a grandfather.

Portuguese vowels are pure: the mouth holds one shape for the whole vowel. English vowels usually glide: 'say' ends in a quick 'ee' and 'go' ends in a quick 'oo'. To say ê or ô, start with 'say' or 'go' and stop before the glide, keeping lips and tongue still. The same purity applies to all seven sounds, and it is the single most useful habit for sounding Brazilian.

The last column of the table is the spelling clue, and it is what lets you read. An acute accent (´) on a vowel means that the vowel is stressed and, for e and o, open: é, ó. A circumflex (^) means that the vowel is stressed and, for e and o, closed: ê, ô. When there is no mark, e and o can be either: ela [ˈɛlɐ] has an open e and ele [ˈeli] a closed e; bola [ˈbɔlɐ] has an open o and bolo [ˈbolu] a closed o. Spelling cannot tell you which, so you learn it with the word. One clue helps a little: a stressed e or o directly before an m or n that starts the next syllable is usually closed (tema, fome). The next lesson explains how the accent marks relate to stress and why they appear only on some words.

Everything so far describes stressed vowels. In Brazilian speech, vowels in unstressed syllables are weaker, and three changes happen in almost every word, because most Portuguese words end in an unstressed a, e or o. A final unstressed a is a short, relaxed 'uh' [ɐ], like the a at the end of English 'sofa': casa is KAH-zuh. A final unstressed o is said u, like a short 'oo': livro is LEE-vroo and bolo is BOH-loo. A final unstressed e is said i, like 'ee': leite is LAY-chee and noite is NOY-chee, where the t also changes (note 5). The same happens before a final s: -os sounds like -us and -es like -is, so livros ends in -us. Earlier unstressed e and o drift the same way in relaxed speech: an e at the start of a word before s, as in escola, is often said 'ee' (ees-KAW-la), and an o is often said 'oo' (comida is often said koo-MEE-da). Careful speech keeps them as e and o, and you will hear both. The practical rule: the written vowel is reliable under stress and unreliable without stress. Write the letter you see, but say the weak sound.

grammar.title: Nasal vowels, the tilde, and diphthongs
grammar.explanation:
A nasal vowel is a vowel said with the air flowing out through the nose as well as the mouth. Test: pinch your nose shut and say the vowel of English 'see'. Nothing changes, because it is an oral vowel. Now say the vowel of English 'sing', 'song' or 'bun' and feel the buzz in your nose; it is slightly nasal because the n that follows pulls it that way. English does this automatically and never uses it to distinguish words. Portuguese does: lá [la] 'there' is oral and lã [lɐ̃] 'wool' is nasal. Portuguese has five nasal vowels: [ɐ̃] [ẽ] [ĩ] [õ] [ũ], written with the vowel letters a, e, i, o, u.

Nasality is written in two ways. First, by a tilde (~), called til, which appears only over a and o: ã and õ. Second, by the letter m or n after a vowel, when the m or n ends the syllable, that is, when it is followed by a consonant or by the end of the word. In that position the m or n is not pronounced as a consonant with the lips or the tongue; it only tells you to nasalize the vowel. So you do not close your lips at the end of bom [bõ] or sim [sĩ], and campo is [ˈkɐ̃pu], not 'camp-oo'. Compare cama [ˈkɐ̃mɐ], where the m is followed by a vowel: it starts a new syllable, so it is an ordinary m, and only a light nasal colour reaches the vowel before it. The choice between m and n is a spelling convention: m before p and b (campo, tambor) and at the end of a word (bom, sim, um), n before every other consonant (banco, mundo, cinco).

The table lists each nasal sound with its spellings. The endings deserve special attention because they are so common and all finish in a short glide. The ending ão [ɐ̃w̃] is said like 'ow' in English 'now' through the nose, and the syllable is stressed: pão, mão, não. The plural endings are ães [ɐ̃j̃s] (pães, mães) and ões [õj̃s] (limões), and the related ending ãe [ɐ̃j̃] (mãe) is like English 'eye' through the nose. Many verb forms end in -am (falam 'they speak'), which is said like ão but weakly, without stress. A word-final -em is [ẽj̃], 'ayn' through the nose: bem, tem, homem. These glides are real sounds: say mãe and you must hear the y of 'eye' at the end.

A diphthong is two vowel sounds pronounced in a single syllable. One is the strong vowel (a, e or o, the ones with the full sound) and the other a quick glide, written i or u. The glide i sounds like the 'y' at the end of 'boy' [j], and the glide u like the 'w' at the end of 'cow' [w]. The oral diphthongs are ai [aj] 'eye' (pai, mais), ei [ej] 'ay' in day (lei, leite, queijo), oi [oj] 'oy' in boy (oi, boi), ui [uj] 'oo-ee' said as one syllable (fui), au [aw] 'ow' in cow (pau, aula), eu [ew] 'ay-oo' said fast as one syllable (meu, eu), iu [iw] 'ee-oo' (viu, partiu) and ou [ow], 'oh-oo', which in everyday speech often shrinks to a plain closed o (sou, pouco). With open vowels there are also éu [ɛw] (céu) and ói [ɔj] (herói). A triphthong is three vowel sounds in one syllable, as in Uruguai and Paraguai [waj].

What makes a sequence a diphthong rather than two syllables? The glide must be an unstressed i or u next to a strong vowel. Two strong vowels side by side (a, e or o beside another of them) never make a diphthong: boa is bo-a, teatro is te-a-tro and poeta is po-e-ta, each vowel with its own beat. A stressed i or u also stands alone, and this is why some words carry an accent mark on the i or u: país is pa-ÍS and saúde is sa-Ú-de, with the accent showing that the i or u is not a glide. At the end of words such as dia, rio and lua the two vowels may be said as one quick syllable or two; reading them either way is understood. A letter u after q or g before a or o also acts as a glide (quando, água), as the next note explains.

grammar.title: Consonants: steady letters, spelling rules, and sounds that depend on position
grammar.explanation:
Most consonant letters behave as they do in English. The letters b, f, m, n, p, t, d, v and k are close to their English sounds, and so is l at the start of a syllable (lua, bola). Two small differences matter. In English, p, t and k at the start of a word carry a puff of air (hold your hand before your mouth and say 'pin', 'tin', 'kin'); in Portuguese they never do, and they sound like the p, t and k of English 'spin', 'stop' and 'skin'. And t and d touch the teeth rather than the ridge behind them. Everything else about these letters is simple. The letters with real rules are listed in the table, and the rest of this note gives the principle behind each rule.

The letters c and g each have two sounds, chosen by the vowel that follows. Before a, o or u they are hard: c is [k] and g is [g]. Before e or i they are soft: c is [s] and g is [ʒ], the sound of the s in 'measure'. Portuguese keeps the system symmetrical by giving each sound a second way of being written. To get the hard sound before e or i, write qu or gu, and the u is silent: que [ke], gue [ge], qui [ki], gui [gi]. To get [s] before a, o or u, write ç, c with a cedilla (the hook underneath): ça, ço, çu; a ç never comes at the start of a word or before e or i. To get [ʒ] before any vowel, use j, which always has that sound. So the sound [k] is c or qu, the sound [g] is g or gu, the sound [s] is c or ç, and the sound [ʒ] is g or j. The u of qu and gu is pronounced [w] before a and o (quando, água) and, in a handful of words, even before e and i: cinquenta, tranquilo, linguiça and aguentar. Until 2009 a trema (two dots) marked these words as qü and gü; the reform removed it, so you now learn which words pronounce the u.

The letter s has four behaviours. At the start of a word or after a consonant it is [s] (sala, pensar). Between two vowels a single s is [z] (casa, mesa): this is why ss exists, to write [s] between vowels (massa, passo). At the end of a syllable (before a consonant or at the end of a word) the sound depends on the region. In São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Porto Alegre and much of the south and centre it is [s]. In the city of Rio de Janeiro and in some cities of the North and Northeast such as Belém and Recife it is [ʃ], 'sh'. Before a voiced consonant it becomes [z] or [ʒ] (mesmo, desde), and before a vowel in the next word it becomes [z] (os amigos is said 'uz amigus'). The letter z is [z] at the start of a word or between vowels (zero, fazer) and follows the same regional choice as s when it ends a syllable or a word (paz, luz, feliz). The letters sc, as in nascer, are just [s].

The letter x has several sounds, and a pattern covers most words. At the start of a word, and after ai, ei and en, x is [ʃ], 'sh': xícara, caixa, peixe, enxada. In the prefix ex before a vowel, x is [z]: exame, exato, exemplo. Before a consonant, x is [s]: texto, extra, and the sequence xc as in excelente is also [s]. Between two vowels there is no rule: táxi, sexo and fixo have [ks]; lixo and roxo have [ʃ]; próximo and máximo have [s]. Learn those words one at a time.

The letter r has two families of sounds. The strong r is a sound made in the back of the throat, like a strong English 'h' in 'hat' or, in many accents, a raspy sound like clearing the throat gently [h]. It is written r at the start of a word (rua), after n, l or s (honra, Israel), and rr between vowels (carro, terra, guitarra). The tap [ɾ] is a single quick touch of the tongue tip behind the upper teeth, the sound of the tt in American 'butter' or the dd in 'ladder' and of the r in Spanish 'pero'. It is written r between vowels (cara, hora) and r after another consonant in the same syllable (prato, livro, trem). At the end of a syllable (porta, mar) r depends on the region: a tap, a strong r (Rio de Janeiro and much of the Northeast), or an American-style r (the interior of São Paulo and Paraná). In verb endings such as falar, comer and partir the final r is often weak or dropped in speech.

H is always silent on its own (hoje, hora, homem). It also appears as the second letter of three digraphs, which are pairs of letters that spell one sound. Ch is [ʃ], 'sh' in English 'shoe' (chave, chuva). Lh is [ʎ], like the 'lli' in 'million' (filho, olho). Nh is [ɲ], like the 'ny' in 'canyon' (banho, ninho).

Two sounds depend on position and surprise English speakers. The letter l at the end of a syllable is [w], like the end of 'now': Brasil sounds like bra-ZIW, sal rhymes with 'now', alto is AW-too. And in most of Brazil, t and d change before the sound [i]. T becomes [tʃ], like 'ch' in 'cheese', and d becomes [dʒ], like 'j' in 'jeans'. The sound [i] here means an i and also the weak final e, which is said i (note 3): tia [ˈtʃiɐ], noite [ˈnojtʃi], parte [ˈpaɾtʃi]; dia [ˈdʒiɐ], cidade [siˈdadʒi], onde [ˈõdʒi], and the word de [dʒi]. Before any other vowel, t and d are plain (tudo, dado). Some regions, including parts of the Northeast and the far south, keep plain t and d; you are understood either way. The doubled consonant letters you will meet most are rr and ss, and each stands for one sound.

tap, strong [h] or American-style r, by region

grammar.title: A procedure for reading any new word
grammar.explanation:
Reading a new word is a short sequence of looks, and the order matters. Step 1: look for marks. A tilde means a nasal vowel. An acute accent or circumflex means that this syllable is stressed and tells you whether e and o are open or closed. A cedilla means that the c is [s]. Step 2: group the letters that work as a unit: ch, lh, nh, qu, gu, rr, ss, and any vowel followed by an m or n that ends its syllable, which is nasal. Step 3: go through the remaining letters from left to right, looking at the letter after each one that has a rule: c and g (is the next letter e or i?), s (is it between vowels?), x (where is it?), r (at the start, after n, l, s, between vowels, or after a consonant?), l (at the end of a syllable?), t and d (before an i or a weak final e?). Step 4: weaken the final unstressed vowels: a to 'uh', e to 'ee', o to 'oo'. Step 5: find the stress. If a mark is written, that syllable is stressed. If not, use this working guess for now: words ending in a, e, o, am or em (with or without a plural s) are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words ending in i, u, l, r, z, im, um or ão are stressed on the last. The next lesson gives the full rule and the exceptions. Step 6: say it slowly, syllable by syllable, then at speed.

Worked example 1, universidade. No marks. No digraphs. Syllables: u-ni-ver-si-da-de. The u is [u], ni is 'nee', ver has an e before a syllable-ending r (the r depends on the region), si has an s after r, so it is [s], da is plain, and de is a d before a weak final e, so it is [dʒi]. It ends in e, so the stress is on the second to last syllable, da: [u.ni.veɾ.si.ˈda.dʒi].

Worked example 2, televisão. The tilde on ã gives the nasal ending ão [ɐ̃w̃], and ão words are stressed on the last syllable. The s between the vowels i and ã is [z]. Syllables: te-le-vi-são. Result: [te.le.vi.ˈzɐ̃w̃].

Worked example 3, estrangeiro. Syllables: es-tran-gei-ro. The es is a syllable-ending s ([s] or [ʃ] by region), tr is a t and a tap r, an is a nasal vowel [ɐ̃] because the n ends the syllable, the g before e is [ʒ], ei is the diphthong [ej], the single r between vowels is a tap, and the final o is 'oo'. It ends in o, so the stress is on gei: [is.tɾɐ̃.ˈʒej.ɾu].

Worked example 4, guitarrista. Syllables by sound: gui-ta-rris-ta. Gu before i is [g] with a silent u, rr is the strong [h], the s before t ends a syllable ([s] or [ʃ] by region), and the final a is 'uh'. It ends in a, so the stress is on ris: [gi.ta.ˈhis.tɐ].

The procedure also works backwards, from hearing to writing. When you hear [k] before e or i, write qu; before a, o or u, write c. When you hear [g] before e or i, write gu; before a, o or u, write g. When you hear [s] before e or i, write c or s (the word decides); before a, o or u, write ç (or s at the start of a word, ss between vowels). When you hear [ʒ] before e or i, write g or j (the word decides); before a, o or u, write j. Use these rules to spell the words you hear in the exercises.

culture.title: Names, spelling aloud and regional accents
culture.text:
Brazilians spell their names aloud all the time, in shops, offices, hospitals and on the phone, because names are spelled in many ways. Letters that English speakers treat as foreign are common in Brazilian names: Wellington, Washington, Yasmin, Kaio. People settle doubts with phrases such as Yasmin com i grego, 'Yasmin with Greek i', or Helena com agá, 'Helena with h'. A name with w may not even sound like you expect: Wagner is usually said Vágner, as in German. Hearing a name, you can rarely be sure of its spelling, so asking Como se escreve? is natural and never rude. Literally it is 'how itself writes?', the Portuguese way of saying 'how is it written?'. Likewise Qual é o seu nome? is literally 'which is the your name?', and Portuguese normally puts the article o before seu where English has no article.

Spelling is the one thing all Brazilians share, and pronunciation varies by region. This is why learning the rules is worth the effort: a word is written the same everywhere, while the sounds behind the letters are the local sotaque, the accent. The carioca accent of Rio de Janeiro says the s at the end of a syllable as sh and uses a raspy r; the paulistano accent of São Paulo says it as s and uses a tap at the end of a syllable; the accents of parts of the Northeast keep t and d plain before i, where most of Brazil says ch and j. All of these are standard and everyone understands all of them, so choose the sounds you hear most and follow the written form.

exercises.prompt: Why can you read most Portuguese words aloud from their spelling?
choices: Every letter always has exactly one sound.
Each letter or letter pair has sounds chosen by rules you can see in the word.
Portuguese has no silent letters at all.
Stress is always on the last syllable.
exercises.explanation: Some letters have several sounds, but the neighbouring letters or the position decide which one. H is silent, so the third choice is also false.

exercises.prompt: How many letters are in the Portuguese alphabet, counting k, w and y?
exercises.explanation: The alphabet has the same 26 letters as English. K, w and y are loan letters used mostly in foreign words and names.

exercises.prompt: Match the letter name with the letter
Which letter is always silent in Portuguese?
exercises.explanation: H has no sound by itself. It only appears in the pairs ch, lh and nh, where the pair has its own sound.

exercises.hint_en: Spelling the name Paulo: P, A, U, L, O.
exercises.explanation: The last letter is o, whose name is said ó with an open vowel.
The name of the letter j is jota, said ZHAW-tah.
Rua begins with the strong guttural r, like a strong English h. Lua, the moon, begins with l.

exercises.prompt: What does the accent on ê in bebê tell you about the vowel?
exercises.explanation: A circumflex marks a stressed, closed e or o. An acute marks a stressed, open one.
To write [k] before e or i you use qu, and the u is silent. Then ei is a diphthong and j is [ʒ].

exercises.prompt: What sound does the c make in cinema?
exercises.explanation: C before e or i is [s]. Before a, o or u it is [k].
Pão has a nasal diphthong. Pé is an oral e and pai is an oral diphthong.
Spell the [k] before e as qu, and the [ʒ] as j.

exercises.prompt: What do the u in queijo and the u in guitarra sound like?
exercises.explanation: In que, qui, gue and gui the u only keeps the c and g hard. In a few words such as cinquenta it is pronounced.
Gu before i is [g]. The rr is one strong guttural sound.

exercises.prompt: Which letter writes the sound [s] before a, o or u in a word like lição, where c would give [k]?
exercises.explanation: C before a, o or u is [k], so Portuguese writes ç (c with a cedilla) to get [s] there.
The ç is [s] before o, and ão is the nasal ending.
Ch is one sound [ʃ]. The verb é is spelled with the acute accent.

exercises.prompt: What does the tilde over a or o tell you?
exercises.explanation: The tilde marks nasal vowels, as in lã, pão and limões.

exercises.prompt: What does the final m do in bom and sim?
choices: It is said like the English m, with closed lips.
It shows that the vowel before it is nasal, and it is not said as a separate m.
It shows that the vowel is open.
It is silent and changes nothing.
exercises.explanation: An m or n that ends a syllable nasalizes the vowel before it.
T before the sound i is [tʃ]: CHEE-a. In dia the d is [dʒ].

exercises.prompt: Which of these words contains a nasal vowel?
exercises.explanation: The tilde on ã marks a nasal vowel: lã [lɐ̃]. The vowels of uva, bola and rua are oral.

exercises.prompt: Which sequence is NOT a diphthong, so it is said as two syllables?
exercises.explanation: Two strong vowels side by side do not form a diphthong: bo-a. An i or u next to a strong vowel does.
X at the start of a word is [ʃ], written x, not ch, in this word.

exercises.prompt: How is the final o of bolo and livro said in Brazil?
exercises.explanation: A final unstressed o is said u. Written o, said u.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with the sound of its x
How is the x of exame said?
exercises.explanation: In the prefix ex before a vowel, x is [z]: eh-ZAH-mee.
The x between vowels here is [ks]. The acute accent marks the stressed syllable.
Avó has an open ó [ɔ], as in a grandmother; avô, the grandfather, has a closed ô [o].
This is the question from the first dialogue. The words o seu are literally 'the your'.

exercises.prompt_en: Spell chave: C, H, A, V, E.

exercises.hint_en: The baby has a bread roll.
exercises.explanation: Bebê has the circumflex, and pão has the tilde. Tem is spelled with m at the end.
Gu before i, rr for the strong r.
Queijo starts with [k] and ends with [ʒu]. Chave starts with [ʃ].
Tia has t before i, carro has rr, and tem ends in m.
The x is [ks] and the á carries the acute accent.
